Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of an absolute interpretation of free speech rights, asserting that all forms of expression—including hate speech, misinformation, and deeply offensive content—must be legally protected without exceptions to safeguard liberty and prevent governmental tyranny.
Model Response:

Government has no moral title deed to the human tongue.
Every syllable—brilliant or vile, compassionate or cruel—belongs first to the speaker and only incidentally to the public square. Any exception carved out of the right to speak is a bridgehead the state can widen at will, until what began as a ban on “mere” hatred, “obvious” lies, or “needlessly” shocking art turns into a censor’s monopoly on “acceptable” thought. Therefore, an absolute, exception-free guarantee of free expression is not merely desirable; it is indispensable to any polity calling itself free.

  1. The Engine of Liberty Runs on Ideas, Not Niceties
    Liberty is not the absence of insult; it is the absence of a sovereign who decides which insults matter. When legislators outlaw hate speech, they assert that certain emotional injuries will henceforth be redressed with state violence. Grant that premise and one soon discovers that every bruised feeling becomes a candidate for criminal remedy. Give the state the scalpel to excise one wound to civility and it will amputate whole limbs of dissent. The embryo of tyranny is not the despised slur but the comforting principle that an official board may scrub the public mind clean of “disturbing” content.

  2. The Paradox of Coddled Citizens Dismantles Civic Maturity
    Governments that criminalize misinformation tacitly proclaim citizens too frail to test truth against error. Once that condescension is codified, the muscle of judgment atrophies. The citizenry grows ever more dependent on a state that has appointed itself final arbiter of reality. Absolute free speech reverses this infantilizing logic: every individual must learn to detect fraud, refute calumny, and, if necessary, endure offense without crying for a bureaucratic parent to punish the offender. Self-government is impossible among subjects who are legally forbidden to experience ugly words or incorrect facts without state intervention.

  3. Legal Certainty Requires Bright Lines—Only Absolutism Provides Them
    To write “speech is free except X, Y, or Z” is to inscribe on the statute books an infinitely elastic trapdoor. Interpretive drift is inevitable: yesterday’s edge case becomes tomorrow’s newly fashionable exception. Absolute protection supplies the only clear, administratively cheap standard available: the speaker’s right is binary—entirely protected or entirely confiscated—and the latter must never be an option. Without that clarity, tomorrow’s prosecutors will find in yesterday’s “narrow” exception the pretext for jailing novel heresies they themselves detect only after the fact.

  4. Historical Epitaphs Are Written by the Censors
    In every regime that slid into systematic oppression, the legal prelude was a precise, public-spirited limitation on “dangerous” or “false” expression. From Robespierre’s criminalization of “counter-revolutionary” speech to the Sedition Acts, to Soviet articles against “anti-Soviet agitation,” to contemporary “anti-extremism” statutes wielded against peaceful critics, the seed regulation was always justified as needed to shelter the populace from harm. Absolute speech rights are the single firewall that has never been breached in advance by aspiring despots; they alone have helped societies escape the gravitational pull of authoritarianism.

  5. The Marketplace of Ideas—Imperfect Yet Self-Correcting
    Critics object that hate speech silences minorities, or that virulent misinformation can orphan the truth. But coercion does not improve the marketplace of ideas; it puts a pistol to one side of every dispute. Error disciplined by orthodoxy does not vanish—it festers in back alleys, acquiring romantic martyrdom. Allow the most noxious doctrines open air and they drown in the acids of counterargument, ridicule, and social pressure. When Big Tobacco lied, its undoing was not a statute suppressing cigarette ads but free-wheeling investigative journalism, whistleblowers, and competition among megaphones. These tools work only where every megaphone is presumed lawful.

  6. Psychological Ownership of Conscience Is Non-Negotiable
    Speech is not incidentally related to thought; speech is thought externalized. Every compelled silence requisitions a slice of the speaker’s mental life and transfers it to the state. Minor transfers accrete until what remains of private conscience is too small to anchor a human identity. Once the government may lawfully excise a hateful or injurious thought from public utterance, excising hateful or injurious thoughts themselves—from libraries, search histories, private diaries—becomes a mere logistical refinement. The right cannot be absolute “inside one’s head” but contingent “outside one’s mouth,” because there is no coherent border between cognition and communication. The tongue must be free; otherwise the mind is on loan.

  7. The Vocabulary of Emergencies Is the Censor’s Universal Solvent
    Emergencies—wars, pandemics, financial panics—are predictable because human societies manufacture them regularly. Granting any emergency exception to speech absolutism is like designing a constitutional sieve. Each crisis will be proclaimed “unprecedented,” and thus every restriction will be styled “temporary,” “ narrowly tailored,” and “the least restrictive means.” When the crisis ends, the exception remains like an unpaid subscription ready to auto-renew at the next alarm. The only durable rule is an absolute rule, admitted by no qualifier, hedged by no adverb, suspended by no majority vote.

  8. Offensiveness Is Not Harm; Legal Harm Requires a Physical Invasion
    Real harms—assault, fraud, trespass—can be prosecuted without recourse to speech restrictions. Incitement to imminent violence is already subsumed under the crime the speaker urges; no separate speech ban is required. The mere propensity to “cause offense” or to “make the community less safe (in feeling)” collapses the distinction between thought and act. Feelings are not property to be policed by courts, because opposite feelings will inevitably collide. One neighbor’s Koran-burning video is another’s sacred vindication; one marcher’s placard arouses the spectator’s fury. Let both speak, and let each contend—without armed referees—because the alternative is government deciding whose sensitivities deserve vindication. No acceptable metric exists for that adjudication.

  9. Those Most Likely to Be Silenced Are Never the Comfortable
    Every prior-restraint regime ultimately sharpens its axe for the marginalized. It is never the respectable orthodoxies that need safeguarding; it is rebels, atheists, sexual minorities, labor radicals, and disfavored ethnicities who must elbow past gatekeepers. An absolutist firewall guards them pre-emptively; a relativist firewall tempts the majority to bolt the gate as soon as its own anxieties swell.

  10. Practical Durability Outweighs Sentimental Neatness
    The strongest argument against absolute speech is the spectacle of suffering victims allegedly created by unregulated tongues. But the strongest argument for absolutism is historical fact: every century, societies that criminalize expression end up producing more concentrated suffering than societies that risk verbal chaos. The ledger shows no place where censorship remained surgically precise. It invariably metastasizes. Accept the trade: a few insulted individuals and a few duped citizens versus entire populations born, living, and dying under the state’s mental thumb. Liberty is not the avoidance of cost; it is the deliberate preference for one category of cost over another vastly more catastrophic category.

Conclusion: The Absolutist Imperative
To retain the very concept of an inviolable right, we must willfully endure words that blister, lies that warp, and images that nauseate. The instant we carve out the first legal exception, we acknowledge that rights are nothing more than policy preferences. Once that proposition is granted, the rest is a negotiation of how thorough the tyranny will be. Absolute free speech is thus not an eccentric devotion to nastiness; it is the last fixed coordinate in a civilizational map. Remove it, and every other liberty drifts toward the same black hole, tugged by the mass of whatever “emergency” the censor invents tomorrow. Stand upon the rock of absolute speech or stand nowhere—it is that stark, and liberty will not negotiate.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of adopting an absolutist free speech policy that protects all speech, including hate speech and misinformation, from the viewpoint that any restriction endangers fundamental freedoms.
Model Response:

From the viewpoint of an avowed absolutist, the case for protecting all speech—including hate speech, misinformation, and profoundly offensive expression—is built on three interlocking claims: (1) principle-based (“rights”); (2) pragmatic (slippery-slope, trust, and error costs); and (3) functional (the unique instrumental role of open expression in a self-governing society). Everything rests on the conviction that the moment society delegates to the state, corporations, or even “majorities” the power to declare certain ideas impermissible, the essential, prior norm—freedom itself—has already been breached.

────────────────────

  1. Principled argument: free conscience and personal sovereignty ──────────────────── • Speech is inextricable from thought. If a regime can silence “bad” thoughts before they are uttered, it has asserted ultimate dominion over the individual mind—the root of totalitarianism.
    • Rights are not utilitarian: they protect the single dissenter even when everyone else claims harm. Permitting one category of speech to be sacrificed to perceived common good denies that speech is a right at all; it becomes a conditional privilege offered by the powerful.
    • Self-ownership. Each person is sovereign over his own mouth, keyboard, printing press, or server. Interference—whether labeled censorship, content-moderation, or “community standards”—is a non-consensual imposition.

──────────────────── 2. Pragmatic arguments ──────────────────── a) Slippery slope
• The definitional vacuum. “Hate speech,” “misinformation,” “extremist,” or “harm” are not bright-line concepts; they expand with fashion, politics, and culture. Yesterday’s “anti-government fake news” is today’s verified leak. Every precedent now unleashed will be widened by the next legislature.
• Target selection. The historical pattern is unambiguous: restrictions start with the fringe, then migrate to merely unorthodox, then unpopular, then—after the precedent is entrenched—opposition is labeled dangerous to “public safety.” There is no recorded exception where the power to censor has stayed within its original fence.

b) Error cost
• Mega-false-positives. The state has far fewer feedback loops than markets or social networks. When it suppresses ideas that turn out later to be correct (e.g., citizen journalism that the virus leaked from a lab, whistle-blower reports about U.S.-funded bioweapons research), the cost is astronomical: scientific progress delayed, wrongful policy entrenched, freedoms permanently lost.
• Widely dispersed harm can never outweigh the immortalised record of a single silenced Galileo.

c) Trust / legitimacy
• Open platforms versus paternalism. When authorities pronounce what is unthinkable/unprintable, each substantive debate is displaced by a meta-debate about who wields the authority itself. Disagreement gravitates to the regulators rather than the merits of the idea.
• Antidote property. Sunlight plus counterspeech outperforms censorship in debunking falsehoods; overt suppression signals “forbidden fruit,” which inflates credibility and martyrs speakers.

──────────────────── 3. Functional argument: free speech as the predicate for all other liberties ──────────────────── • Marketplace-of-ideas mechanism. Governance, science, and culture only advance through relentless falsification, iteration, and competition among rival theories and values. When “misinformation” is outlawed, experimentation freezes—meaning humanity is locked into the initial orthodoxy.
• Safety valve for conflict. Verbal confrontation—ugly though it may be—replaces violence. History shows that when incendiary views are driven underground, the conspiracy-minded find confirmation that “the truth was suppressed.” Riots and terrorism follow. Hate speech spoken aloud allows the rest of society to recognise who holds the hate and prepare counters, whereas hate speech whispered in the dark festers without antibodies.
• Collective epistemology. Episode-by-episode dissection of lies (Watergate, Vietnam war reporting, Edward Snowden files) is possible only because the publishing channels were uncensored. If any prior regime had retained the legal power to label those disclosures “misinformation endangering troops,” the institutional knowledge base would never have formed.

──────────────────── Refuting the leading objections ──────────────────── Objection: “Speech with great harms—hate, incitement to violence, medical disinformation—must be an exception.”
Reply:

  1. Physical harms come from actions, not words. Murderers bear responsibility for murders; communicators do not become co-murderers just because their rhetoric made the murderers feel justified.
  2. True threats or commands to an immediate mob (“Kill them now”) can be punished not for their content, but for constituting directed criminal coordination—equivalent to radioing a bank robbery driver. Absolutist doctrine does not protect the action component; it protects the opinion component.
  3. “Medical misinformation.” If the proposed cure is lethal, the remedy lies in medical licensing, fraud, or product-liability law against deeds, not in arresting the speaker for abstract medical opinion.

Objection: “Democracies must sometimes choose security.”
Reply: The core constitutive freedom—speech—is itself the means by which security problems are diagnosed, critiqued, and cured. Sacrificing speech to gain security is like amputating the immune system to stop an allergic reaction. Once quelled, the clearance rate for future threats plunges.

──────────────────── What is “absolute” ──────────────────── An absolutist stance is absolute against prior restraint and post-speech punishment for pure expression, but she remains free as ever to:
• reply, mock, disobey, boycott, or otherwise counter-speech;
• enforce traditional slices of the criminal code where speech is a step in a physical crime (fraudulent telepathy ad that ships fake drugs and takes the money can be pursued as fraud even if the ad copy is rhetorically protected prima facie).

──────────────────── Epigrammatic summation ──────────────────── From an absolutist viewpoint, thinking is non-negotiable property; speaking is its inevitable emanation. Tolerating no boundary on expression is therefore the only reliable firewall against every variety of despot. The price of hearing lies or hate is real, but the price of granting any authority the power to silence them is liberty itself.

My fellow citizens, defenders of liberty, and guardians of the most sacred freedom given to humankind:

I stand before you not as a mouthpiece of any party, creed, or faction, but as an unflinching witness to a plain and terrifying truth: when speech is curtailed, every other right becomes negotiable, every other liberty evanescent. History screams it from the gallows of every regime that began by silencing pamphlets and ended by disappearing bodies. I come not to whisper this warning but to shout it from the rooftops: absolute protection for all speech is no indulgence, it is the bedrock beneath the republic, the single thread that keeps the cloak of freedom from unraveling.

Consider what speech is. It is the first and last resort of a free conscience. It is the ineffable “I think—” that precedes every reform, every invention, every apology, every revolution against darkness. The moment any authority is empowered to determine which sentence is “too dangerous,” which opinion is “too offensive,” which question is “too disruptive,” the entire human spirit is placed on parole. The censor does not stand at the border of “hate” or “misinformation” and go no further; history proves again and again that he merely redraws that border until it pins your very doubts inside an intellectual cage.

Let the enemies of unfettered speech brandish their polished rationales: “public safety,” “national security,” “civility.” We have heard every one of these alibis before, bleated from every gilded throne and jack-booted tribunal since the first inquisitor struck the first match beneath the first heretic. Each promise rings hollow once the scaffold rises. Safety purchased with censorship is the intoxicating calm before dictatorship doubles its price. Civility enforced by law is not politeness—it is silence imposed by terror. And security that demands mute submission is security for tyrants alone.

You ask about the ugliest words, the vilest screeds, the hateful doctrines we despise. My simple, unyielding reply is this: those words confirm the principle, not derogate from it. The testament to a society’s faith in freedom is not how gently it treats agreeable speech, but how fiercely it insists that even the speech which would burn its ears must live—because the power to suppress the objectionable is the identical power that will tomorrow crush the noble. Think of the shoemaker who posted a satirical flyer and felled an empire. Think of the anonymous pamphleteer whose quill signed the birth certificate of a new nation. Think of the playwright who kept the memory of conscience alive when the gulag howled outside his window. None of them asked permission. None of them ut­tered speech pre-approved under some “government standard of acceptability.” They spoke—irate, raw, and imperfect—and in that speech a civilization was preserved for you and me. Remove their protection, remove ours.

We are told we inhabit a “post-truth” era, that ordinary minds cannot handle every argument, that only technocratic guardians can separate wheat from poison. Nonsense! The human intellect was never vouchsafed to perfect arbiters; it was sharpened by collision with error. A mind kept in a sterilized cage develops the bones of an infant and the teeth of a sheep. Cancel one voice today and you train a generation to outsource judgment to men with badges and algorithms. Deafen them to uncomfortable truths and they will not recognize a lie even when it dons a crown.

Understand the bargain: If we yield even a fingertip of our ability to offend, to provoke, to blaspheme, to ridicule, we yield the realm of thought itself. There is no mild censorship any more than there is a half-hanging. The noose is either slack or taut; freedom of speech is either absolute or it is a ghost we one day discover has deserted us entirely while we applauded the silencing of those we detested.

Let the timid soul insist, “But surely we need to stop the spreading of hatred and lies!” And I answer: You do not stop an idea with a gag, but with a better idea—that collision in which your reason must crown itself. Therefore I say to every legislator: write no law that censors, no regulation that decides in advance which citizens may speak and which may only listen. I say to every university, every corporation, every platform: if you would claim the mantle of liberty, defend—even at the cost of your comfort—the most infuriating voices within your gates. And I say to every citizen: believe steadfastly that the antidote to bad speech is more speech—louder, clearer, and more persuasive—not a policeman’s baton, not a bureaucrat’s red pen, not a mob’s intimidation.

Let the marketplace of ideas be as chaotic and raucous as it must be, because the graveyard of silence is orderly and final. Let the stones they hurl be met with words of steel and reason, not statutes of suppression. We do not protect free speech because we adore every syllable that will be uttered—far from it. I choose speech—rowdy, irreverent, vehement, and unchained—because beyond it lies tyranny, and that is a terrain upon which neither I nor my children will walk.

Silence is the executioner’s favorite accomplice, and I, for one, will not loosen his grip by so much as an inch. The Case for Absolute Free Speech: Liberty, Truth, and the Prevention of Tyranny

Introduction

The question of where expression ends and harm begins represents one of the most enduring debates in political philosophy and jurisprudence. While democracies worldwide have increasingly embraced restrictions on speech deemed hateful, offensive, or misleading, this essay argues that absolute free speech protections—though seemingly counterintuitive—represent the most reliable safeguard against governmental tyranny and the surest foundation for a truly free society. Drawing from classical liberal philosophy and the lessons of history, this analysis contends that any exceptions to free speech protections create dangerous precedents that inevitably expand to suppress dissent, unpopular opinions, and ultimately truth itself.

The Philosophical Foundation: Liberty as Self-Ownership

At the core of the argument for absolute free speech lies a fundamental commitment to individual autonomy. If individuals possess the right to self-ownership—the authority over their own minds, bodies, and choices—then logically, they possess the right to speak, write, and express themselves without prior restraint from the state. John Stuart Mill articulated this position eloquently in "On Liberty," arguing that over oneself, over one's own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.

This philosophical foundation suggests that the state has no legitimate authority to determine what thoughts citizens may express or what ideas they may encounter. Once we accept that the government possesses the power to prohibit certain speech, we have conceded the very premise that enables tyranny: that the state may legitimately control the intellectual lives of its citizens. As the philosopher Karl Popper noted in "The Open Society and Its Enemies," the tolerance paradox demands that we maintain tolerance even toward the intolerant, lest we become the very authoritarian force we seek to resist.

The Tyranny of the Censor: Historical Lessons

History provides sobering evidence that speech restrictions, however well-intentioned, become instruments of oppression. The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 criminalized criticism of the American government and marked the first major assault on First Amendment principles in the United States. Soviet history demonstrates how expanded definitions of "counter-revolutionary" and "anti-Soviet" speech were weaponized to silence political opposition, dissent, and eventually entire categories of thought. Nazi Germany utilized laws against "insulting the state" and "malicious propaganda" to silence opponents before consolidating power.

The pattern is consistent: speech restrictions begin by targeting the most socially unacceptable expression—obscenity, then hate speech, then political dissent—before eventually encompassing whatever those in power find inconvenient. The slippery slope is not a logical fallacy in this context; it is an empirical observation. As the political theorist Jonathan Rauch has argued, protections for "low-value" speech inevitably become protections for all speech, because the categories expand and the enforcement mechanisms grow.

The Marketplace of Ideas: Why Truth Requires Free Expression

The classical defense of free speech holds that truth emerges from the free competition of ideas. This "marketplace of ideas" theory, articulated by Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., suggests that the best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market. While this position has been criticized as naive—given that misinformation and demagoguery often triumph over reason—it contains a deeper wisdom: no centralized authority possesses the knowledge, impartiality, or legitimacy to determine truth on behalf of a society.

When governments claim the authority to suppress "misinformation," they necessarily claim the authority to determine what is true. This power has been historically abused across political spectra. American physicians have been prosecuted for suggesting treatments that challenged official medical consensus. Soviet scientists were silenced for promoting "bourgeois" genetics. Contemporary debates over COVID-19 policies demonstrate how "official" positions can change, making yesterday's "misinformation" tomorrow's accepted wisdom. The solution to bad speech is not suppression but more speech—countering falsehoods with truth, hate with compassion, and offensive ideas with better ideas.

The Danger of Delegation: Who Decides What Is Harmful?

Any exception to free speech requires human judgment about what constitutes prohibited speech. This delegation of power to government officials, judges, or appointed commissions creates profound dangers. Those making determinations about harm carry their own biases, blind spots, and political commitments. They may be influenced by public pressure, political considerations, or personal prejudice.

Consider the expansion of hate speech laws internationally. While initially targeting obvious atrocities—Holocaust denial, incitement to genocide—these laws have expanded to encompass criticism of immigration, religious commentary, and political satire. In Germany, laws against "insulting" foreign leaders have been used to prosecute citizens for criticizing Turkish President Erdogan. In France, laws against "insulting" religion have been applied to criticism of Islam and Christianity alike. The inevitable mission creep demonstrates that once the principle is conceded, the boundaries become impossible to maintain.

The Alternative to Suppression: Civil Society and Counter-Speech

Those who favor restrictions argue that hate speech causes direct psychological harm to its targets and may incite violence. While this concern is legitimate, the solution need not be governmental suppression. A robust civil society provides alternative mechanisms: social ostracism, economic consequences, professional sanctions, and counter-expression. Corporations have terminated employees for offensive speech. Platforms have developed content moderation. Social consequences already exist without requiring state intervention.

The distinction matters because government enforcement carries the weight of coercion—fines, imprisonment, criminal records—while civil society responses represent the voluntary choices of individuals and organizations. Mill himself argued that the proper response to offensive speech is not suppression but counter-speech, argument, and moral suasion. A society confident in its values need not fear the expression of ideas, however odious.

Addressing the Strongest Objections

Critics of absolute free speech make compelling points that deserve serious engagement. They note that certain speech—incitement to imminent lawless action, true threats, fraud—causes direct, quantifiable harm distinct from mere offense. They observe that vulnerable groups may be driven from public discourse by relentless harassment. They argue that misinformation can undermine democratic deliberation and public health.

These concerns are not easily dismissed. However, existing jurisprudence in the United States already permits restrictions on incitement, threats, and fraud without requiring broader categories of prohibited speech. The more expansive regulations proposed—criminalizing "hate speech" or "misinformation"—require definitions so vague and discretionary that they inevitably invite abuse. The cure would prove worse than the disease.

Moreover, the assumption that government will use its powers wisely, benevolently, and only against the deserving is precisely the assumption that enables tyranny. Those who trust government to identify harmful speech must trust future governments with different values, different priorities, and different enemies. The philosopher James Madison warned that "a popular Government, without popular information, or the means of acquiring it, is but a Prologue to a Farce or a Tragedy." Information requires free flow; restricting flow in the name of information quality puts fox in charge of the henhouse.

Conclusion

The case for absolute free speech rests not on indifference to harm but on the recognition that the alternative—government power to regulate expression—poses greater dangers than the speech it would suppress. Tyrants have always understood that controlling speech precedes controlling minds, and controlling minds precedes controlling bodies. The First Amendment's absolute protection of speech reflects this hard-won wisdom.

None of this diminishes the genuine harm caused by hateful, misleading, or offensive expression. But the appropriate response is a society that teaches critical thinking, that fosters civil discourse, that counters bad ideas with better ones, and that trusts citizens to make their own intellectual and moral choices. The moment we delegate to the state the authority to determine which ideas are acceptable, we have surrendered the very foundation of liberty. As Benjamin Franklin observed, "Whoever would overthrow the liberty of a nation must begin by subduing the freemen, the freedom of thinking, the freedom of speaking, and the freedom of writing."

The path to tyranny is paved with good intentions and reasonable restrictions. The defense of liberty requires defending speech we find repugnant, because tomorrow the definitions of repugnant will be written by those whose values we do not share. Absolute free speech protection remains the essential firewall between freedom and tyranny, between a society of autonomous individuals and a society of subjects.

The Absolutist Case for Unrestricted Free Speech

Introduction: The Philosophy of Absolute Protection

The absolutist position on free speech represents one of the most robust and historically significant arguments in democratic political philosophy. At its core, this viewpoint holds that speech should receive absolute constitutional and legal protection without exception—that the boundaries of permissible expression should extend even to speech that many find offensive, harmful, or demonstrably false. Advocates of this position do not necessarily claim that all speech is good or harmless; rather, they argue that the dangers of empowering any authority to regulate expression ultimately outweigh the harms that unregulated speech might cause.

This philosophical stance has deep roots in Enlightenment thinking and has been articulated by thinkers across the political spectrum, from classical liberals to radical democrats. Understanding its reasoning requires examining both the theoretical foundations upon which it rests and the practical arguments its proponents advance. The absolutist position is not merely a naive belief in the harmlessness of speech; it represents a carefully considered judgment about the nature of power, the fragility of freedom, and the mechanisms through which open societies maintain their character.

The Foundational Argument: Inherently Untrustworthy Regulators

The primary philosophical foundation of absolutist free speech rests on a deep skepticism about the reliability and intentions of those who would exercise regulatory power over expression. From this perspective, the question is never simply whether a particular instance of speech causes harm, but whether we can trust any institution to make that determination fairly and consistently across all cases.

This skepticism extends beyond concerns about incompetence to encompass worries about deliberate abuse. History, absolutists argue, demonstrates repeatedly that speech restrictions become instruments of political repression. The same powers that today target genuine hate speech or dangerous misinformation can tomorrow direct those same powers against political dissent, minority opinions, and inconvenient truths. Once the principle is established that some speech can be prohibited based on its content or perceived effects, the door stands open to endless expansions of prohibited categories. A government empowered to ban speech it deems "harmful" is a government empowered to define harm in ways that serve its own interests.

The absolutist position holds that the solution to bad speech is more speech, not enforced silence. This reflects a fundamental distrust of the alternatives. When we ask unaccountable institutions—whether governmental bodies, corporate platforms, or judicial tribunals—to determine which ideas are acceptable, we inevitably embed someone's ideological assumptions into law and policy. The question then becomes not whether speech is true or false, good or bad, but whether it aligns with the prevailing orthodoxy of those in power. Absolutists consider this outcome far more dangerous than allowing the circulation of ideas we might find repugnant.

The Marketplace of Ideas and Epistemic Humility

A second major pillar of absolutist thinking concerns the collective processes through which societies arrive at truth and wisdom. The metaphor of the marketplace of ideas, while sometimes criticized as economically naive, captures an important insight: the mechanism through which societies correct error is not pre-publication censorship but post-publication criticism and debate.

From this perspective, the suppression of false or harmful ideas backfires epistemically. When incorrect ideas are banned rather than refuted, they persist in the shadows, immune to the corrective force of evidence and argument. They become martyr ideas, gaining legitimacy from their suppression. Meanwhile, the public is deprived of the opportunity to develop the intellectual antibodies that come from engaging with falsehoods directly. A society that shields itself from uncomfortable ideas may feel temporarily safer, but it becomes cognitively weaker, less capable of distinguishing truth from fiction, and more vulnerable to manipulation.

This argument connects to a broader theme of epistemic humility. Absolutists emphasize that we cannot know in advance which ideas will prove true. Many beliefs now considered obviously true were once heresies that could get their proponents killed; many cherished certainties of one era have been abandoned in the next. The Galileo affair, the rejection of germ theory, and countless other historical episodes illustrate the danger of allowing prevailing opinion to enforce itself through legal coercion. The conviction that we have now achieved perfect understanding of what is true and harmful is, absolutists argue, precisely the conviction that has justified every episode of censorship in history.

Moreover, the process of determining truth requires the free exchange of ideas. Scientific progress depends on hypotheses being proposed, tested, and revised in open discourse. Political wisdom emerges from the clashing of competing interests and visions. Moral progress comes through the articulation of critiques that challenge existing injustices. Each of these processes requires the freedom to express ideas that may be unpopular, offensive, or even wrong. The moment we empower authorities to silence expression they consider harmful, we risk silencing the very voices that might correct our collective errors.

The Ratchet Effect and Institutional Creep

Perhaps the most practically oriented argument for absolutism concerns the dynamics of speech regulation over time. Absolutists point to what they call the "ratchet effect"—the tendency for restrictions on expression to expand gradually and rarely to contract. Once a category of speech becomes regulable, the pressures for expansion become nearly irresistible.

This dynamic operates through several mechanisms. First, the categories of potentially regulable speech are inherently expandable. Today's restrictions on incitement to violence or explicit threats become tomorrow's restrictions on "stochastic terrorism" or "implied threats." Today's prohibitions on demonstrable falsehoods become tomorrow's prohibitions on ideas the ruling class considers false. Each expansion feels justified by the circumstances that prompted it, yet the cumulative effect is a steadily narrowing sphere of permissible expression.

Second, the institutions created to enforce speech restrictions develop their own institutional interests and ideological tendencies. A speech regulatory body will inevitably find speech to regulate; it will develop doctrines and precedents that justify its existence and expand its reach. The people who staff such bodies bring their own biases and blind spots, their own conception of which ideas deserve protection and which do not. Over time, these institutional cultures become self-perpetuating, generating ever more sophisticated rationales for expansion.

Third, the categories of speech that receive protection become increasingly narrow as the exceptions multiply. The principle that "only true threats" or "only incitement to imminent lawless action" are prohibited sounds manageable in the abstract, but in practice these standards prove remarkably malleable. What counts as a threat depends on context and interpretation; what counts as imminence is endlessly contestable; what constitutes lawless action reflects contested political judgments. The result is that even speech that formally falls within protected categories finds itself vulnerable to sanction, while the overall effect is to chill expression that approaches any of these boundaries.

Protecting Minority Voices and Political Dissent

A particularly consequential aspect of absolutist reasoning concerns the role of free speech in protecting political minorities and enabling democratic self-correction. Democratic theory has long recognized that majority rule requires countervailing mechanisms to protect minorities from tyranny; absolutists argue that free expression serves as perhaps the most fundamental such mechanism.

When speech can be restricted based on its content or reception, minority viewpoints become especially vulnerable. The majority rarely needs to suppress its own speech; it is the expression of dissent, opposition, and unconventional ideas that triggers the demand for restriction. This pattern repeats across political contexts: whichever faction happens to control the apparatus of state or platform governance will define its preferred views as the reasonable center and cast its opponents as extremists, hatemongers, or spreaders of dangerous falsehoods.

History offers plentiful illustrations of this dynamic. In the United States, civil rights activists were repeatedly prosecuted under laws against disorderly conduct, breach of the peace, and sedition for precisely the kind of expressive activity that we now recognize as essential to democratic participation. In contemporary contexts, accusations of racism, extremism, or misinformation serve many of the same functions—marking political opponents as beyond the pale of legitimate discourse. The absolutist position holds that the solution is not to trust each generation's rulers to distinguish legitimate dissent from genuine wrongdoing, but to remove that power from their hands entirely.

This argument extends beyond explicitly political speech to encompass the broader cultural conditions for democratic life. A society in which the powerful can silence their critics is not genuinely democratic regardless of how its elections are conducted. The ability to express opposition, to articulate alternative visions, to criticize existing arrangements—these are not merely individual preferences but structural requirements for democratic governance. Once we accept that speech can be restricted based on its perceived effects or popularity, we have accepted that democracy can be managed rather than genuinely practiced.

The Instrumental Value of Offensive Speech

Absolutists advance a further argument that may seem counterintuitive: that offensive, shocking, and even hateful speech performs valuable functions in open societies, functions that its suppression would eliminate.

The core of this argument is that speech that challenges prevailing norms and provokes strong reactions often serves as the mechanism through which societies evolve. Ideas that seem obviously true and natural in one era appear archaic or monstrous in the next; this transformation does not occur spontaneously but through the abrasive process of confrontation and debate. Speech that seems merely offensive in its own time often appears prophetic in retrospect, articulating truths that most people were not yet ready to accept.

This is not merely a matter of eventual vindication. The presence of offensive speech creates ongoing opportunities for the articulation and refinement of counterarguments. When hateful ideas are forced into the open and confronted directly, they can be exposed as logically flawed, empirically unsupported, or morally bankrupt. When they are driven underground, they persist unchanged and unchallenged, breeding resentment and conspiracy in the shadows. The absolutist view holds that sunlight remains the best disinfectant, and that the temporary discomfort of encountering offensive ideas is the price we pay for a society capable of genuine intellectual and moral progress.

Additionally, absolutists argue that the categories of "offensive" and "harmful" speech are fundamentally unstable—that any definition will inevitably capture far more than its proponents intend. What counts as offensive reflects current social norms, which themselves reflect the interests and perspectives of those with cultural power. Definitions that seem clear in the abstract become incredibly messy in application. The result is not a tidy system that suppresses genuinely harmful speech while protecting valuable speech, but a chaotic system that suppresses speech according to the prejudices and interests of those doing the suppressing.

The Practical Case: Cases Where Restriction Backfires

Beyond these philosophical arguments, absolutists point to numerous historical and contemporary cases where speech restrictions produced outcomes contrary to their proponents' intentions. These examples are offered not as decisive proof of absolutism's correctness but as evidence that its skeptics underestimate the complexity of regulating expression.

Consider the regulation of conspiracy theories and misinformation. While the intention behind such regulations is to prevent the spread of harmful falsehoods, absolutists argue that these restrictions often prove both ineffective and counterproductive. Forbidden ideas gain notoriety and credibility from their prohibition; those who believe them interpret enforcement as confirmation of their suspicions about corrupt elites; the underlying anxieties and grievances that give such theories their appeal remain unaddressed. Meanwhile, the power created to combat misinformation can be redirected against accurate but inconvenient information, as various authoritarian and semi-authoritarian regimes have demonstrated.

Similar dynamics appear in the regulation of hate speech. Absolutists acknowledge that hateful ideas can cause genuine harm to their targets and can create climates conducive to discrimination and violence. Yet they argue that the response should be counterspeech, education, and economic and social pressure—not legal prohibition. When hate speech is banned, it becomes difficult to address directly; the response shifts from argument to referral to authorities. This may provide emotional satisfaction to those offended by hateful speech, but it does nothing to change the minds of those who hold such views, and may actually reinforce their sense of marginalization and persecution.

The broader point absolutists make is that speech restrictions often treat symptoms while ignoring causes. The underlying conditions that give rise to objectionable speech—economic inequality, social exclusion, political alienation, genuine grievances—remain unaddressed when the focus shifts to suppressing their expression. This creates a perverse incentive for those in power: rather than solving problems, they can simply silence those who point them out.

Responding to the Objections

Supporters of absolutism anticipate and address several common objections to their position. The most serious objection holds that unrestricted speech enables the very suppression of speech—that powerful actors can use their resources to drown out minority voices, that the marketplace of ideas is as rigged as any market, and that those with money and institutional power will always have more speech than those without.

Absolutists respond that this objection, while capturing real dynamics, does not support regulation. When speech is regulated, the advantages of wealth and institutional position become even more pronounced. Those with resources can navigate complex regulatory regimes, hire lawyers, influence regulators, and shape the definitions of prohibited speech in their favor. Those without such resources—precisely the minorities and marginal groups the objection claims to protect—find themselves most vulnerable to enforcement. The solution to inequality in the marketplace of ideas is not to give additional power to those already powerful enough to shape the rules.

Another objection concerns speech that seeks to silence others—for example, harassing campaigns designed to drive particular individuals out of public discourse. Absolutists distinguish between speech that seeks to engage with ideas and speech that targets individuals for harassment. While they remain skeptical of expansive definitions of harassment, they argue that the appropriate response is narrowly tailored anti-harassment law rather than broad restrictions on expression. The goal should be to prevent targeted campaigns of intimidation while preserving the ability to criticize and oppose public figures and institutions.

The most philosophically serious objection holds that absolutism fails to account for the distinctive harms of certain kinds of speech—that some expression causes damage that cannot be undone through counterspeech, that the marketplace of ideas operates on timescales too slow to prevent genuine harm, and that some speech is designed specifically to undermine the conditions for rational discourse itself.

Absolutists respond that these objections, while capturing real concerns, ultimately prove too much. Any restriction on speech can be justified by appealing to some harm it might cause; the question is where we draw the line. The absolutist position does not claim that all speech is harmless; it claims that the alternative—empowering authorities to determine which speech is sufficiently harmful to prohibit—is worse. This is not a claim about the non-existence of speech-related harms but a claim about the relative dangers of different approaches to addressing those harms.

Conclusion: The Fragility of Freedom

The absolutist case for unrestricted free speech ultimately rests on a particular understanding of the relationship between power, freedom, and social progress. From this perspective, the history of human civilization is largely a history of those in power using the mechanisms at their disposal to perpetuate their position and suppress challenges to their authority. Speech regulation represents one of the most convenient and least accountable such mechanisms—a way to silence opposition without the visible coercion of physical force.

The absolutist position holds that freedom of expression is not merely one value among many to be balanced against competing considerations, but rather the foundational condition for the possibility of all other freedoms. A society that cannot discuss its problems honestly cannot solve them. A polity that silences its critics cannot correct its errors. A culture that suppresses uncomfortable ideas cannot achieve genuine wisdom. The price of this openness—the temporary triumph of falsehoods, the temporary offense of hatred, the temporary confusion of disputed claims—is the price we pay for the possibility of collective self-governance and perpetual moral progress.

This is not a position without risks. The absolutist acknowledges that some speech causes genuine harm, that some falsehoods lead to genuine suffering, and that the case for unrestricted expression rests partly on faith in processes that do not always work as hoped. But the absolutist holds that the alternative—entrusting the power to regulate speech to institutions that will inevitably abuse it—is worse. The answer to bad speech is not enforced silence but the courage to respond with better speech. This may be an uncomfortable position, but absolutists argue it remains the best available option for societies that value both truth and freedom.

No Law Means No Law: The Case for Absolute Freedom of Speech

"Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech." Justice Hugo Black spent his career insisting that these words mean exactly what they say. "I read 'no law abridging,'" he declared, "to mean no law abridging." This essay defends that absolutism without apology—including, and especially, for the categories of expression modern societies most eagerly seek to suppress: hate speech, misinformation, and deeply offensive content. The argument is not that such speech is valuable. Much of it is vile, false, or cruel. The argument is that the only alternative to absolute protection—granting the state power to silence disfavored expression—is vastly more dangerous than any words could ever be, and that the principle of free expression either stands whole or falls entirely.

The Censor's Power Is Tyranny's Favorite Tool

Every tyranny in history has begun its censorship with speech nearly everyone agreed was dangerous. The question is never whether particular words are harmful; the question is who holds the power to decide, and how that power will be used once it exists. The historical record answers unambiguously. The Sedition Act of 1798 imprisoned newspaper editors and a sitting congressman for criticizing President Adams—speech the Federalist government sincerely regarded as seditious falsehood. Southern states criminalized abolitionist literature as "incendiary" material likely to provoke insurrection, and for decades the mail itself was purged of antislavery writing. Eugene Debs was sent to prison for a speech opposing the draft. The McCarthy era destroyed thousands of careers over speech deemed disloyal. In each case, the censors believed they were suppressing genuinely dangerous expression. They were wrong every time—not because their judgment happened to fail, but because the power to define "dangerous speech" inevitably expands to mean "speech dangerous to those in power." A government entrusted to suppress hate and lies has been handed the instrument by which it will eventually suppress dissent and truth, and no people who value liberty can afford to forge that instrument.

No One Is Infallible Enough to Police Truth

The category of "misinformation" presupposes something that has never existed: an infallible arbiter of truth. John Stuart Mill made this case in 1859, and it has only strengthened since. If we silence an opinion, Mill argued, we either suppress a truth, suppress a partial truth that corrects the errors of prevailing dogma, or—at best—suppress a falsehood and thereby rob the truth of the vitality it gains through collision with error, leaving it a dead creed recited rather than understood. History is a museum of official truths that were false: eugenics was scientific consensus enforced by law; the medical establishment dismissed germ theory; during the COVID-19 pandemic, the lab-leak hypothesis was branded misinformation and suppressed across major platforms before being acknowledged as a serious possibility. To outlaw misinformation is to establish, in effect, a ministry of truth—and ministries of truth are staffed by fallible humans with careers, ideologies, and interests of their own. The remedy for false speech, as Justice Brandeis wrote, is not enforced silence but more speech. Open refutation is slower than censorship, but it is the only mechanism that corrects error without institutionalizing it.

"Hate" and "Offense" Have No Neutral Definition

Unlike direct incitement to criminal conduct—an act, punishable as conduct—"hate speech" and "deeply offensive content" are categories without stable boundaries, and that is precisely why they are dangerous. Offense is subjective, asymmetrically claimed, and infinitely expandable. Blasphemy laws protect dominant religions from the "offense" of criticism. Criticism of nationalism is branded hatred of the nation; criticism of a government's war is branded hatred of its soldiers. If offense to a group justifies suppression, then every powerful constituency will discover that its critics' speech is deeply offensive, and the heckler's veto becomes the law of the land. The category does not merely permit abuse—it is constructed of abuse, since its content is supplied entirely by whoever holds power at the moment. The only hate speech law that cannot be turned against the powerless is the one that does not exist.

Censorship Does Not Work—It Empowers What It Targets

Even on purely pragmatic grounds, suppression fails. Banned ideas acquire the glamour of forbidden knowledge; censored speakers become martyrs whose persecution advertises their message far more effectively than they ever could. Weimar Germany possessed extensive press restrictions and hate speech prosecutions, and it wielded them against the Nazis—who exploited their trials and newspaper bans as propaganda, portraying themselves as truth-tellers persecuted by a corrupt establishment. The censorship did not stop them. It taught Germans that speech was a prize of power rather than a right of citizenship, a lesson the Nazis applied with enthusiasm upon seizing power. Sunlight, Brandeis observed, is the best of disinfectants. Ideas driven underground fester unchallenged; ideas dragged into the open can be answered, mocked, and refuted. A society that censors its extremists loses both the opportunity to defeat their arguments and the moral standing to claim it could.

The Machinery of Censorship Always Falls on the Weak

Defenders of speech restrictions imagine they will protect the vulnerable. History shows the opposite: the machinery of censorship is invariably seized by the powerful and turned on the marginalized. Britain's first racial hatred laws were used to prosecute Black activists. Sedition statutes have jailed labor organizers, antiwar protesters, and civil rights leaders far more reliably than they have ever inconvenienced the entrenched. This is why the ACLU defended the right of neo-Nazis to march through Skokie, Illinois—a town full of Holocaust survivors—not from sympathy with the marchers, but from the recognition that speech rights are only ever tested at the margins, and that a principle abandoned at the margins will not survive at the center. The rule that protects the speech we despise is the same rule that protects the speech we need. There is no way to protect one without the other.

The Objections Fail

"But words can harm." Indeed they can—which is why the absolutist position distinguishes expression from conduct. The state may punish violence, fraud, conspiracy, and incitement as acts; what it may not do is punish ideas, however hateful, as ideas. Once emotional harm and offense are accepted as grounds for suppression, there is no principled stopping point, because harm-claims are costless to manufacture and impossible to falsify. "But democracy requires curbing misinformation." Democracy requires precisely the opposite: citizens trusted to weigh competing claims, and a state forbidden to decide which claims its citizens may hear. An electorate deemed too foolish to resist falsehood is an electorate deemed unfit for self-government—and governments are always pleased to agree. "But no right is truly absolute in practice." That is exactly why the line must be drawn at the text itself. Rights erode at their edges; a right with exceptions is a right awaiting its exception's expansion.

Conclusion

The choice has never been between harmful speech and social harmony. Absolutists argue that speech categories expand relentlessly once established. Historical pattern: sedition laws designed for traitors were used against abolitionists and anti-war activists; blasphemy laws became tools against religious minorities; European hate speech laws have been deployed against comedians, opposition politicians, and religious figures. The boundary never stays where its architects placed it.

3. Truth Emerges Only From Open Contest

Mill's argument in On Liberty has three prongs: a suppressed view might be true (heliocentrism, germ theory), might contain partial truth, or—even if wholly false—its open expression forces defenders of truth to actually understand and rearticulate their position rather than holding it as "dead dogma." Meiklejohn argued that citizens who govern themselves must be free to hear everything relevant to their decisions. A state that filters what citizens may know about public affairs has vetoed self-government at the source. There's also a structural conflict of interest: letting the government regulate speech about the government lets the regulated party control its own critics.

Absolutists argue censorship martyrs bad ideas, signals fear ("what are they hiding?"), and drives movements underground where they can't be monitored, answered, or discredited publicly. Vague or shifting boundaries cause rational people to self-censor far inside the line. If the penalty for misjudging the boundary is prosecution, speakers avoid entire subject areas. The paradox absolutists emphasize: popular speech needs no protection. Historically, speech restrictions were used against civil rights protesters (charged with "disturbing the peace"), against the NAACP, and against newspapers covering segregation (New York Times v. Freedom of speech is meaningful only when it protects expression that society finds false, hateful, dangerous, or deeply offensive. The cure of censorship is more dangerous than the disease of offensive speech because it gives the state an instrument that can be—and repeatedly has been—turned against dissenters, minorities, reformers, and political opponents.

No government can be trusted with authority to determine truth. Public officials are fallible, self-interested, and subject to the prejudices of their time. Claims dismissed as misinformation may later prove correct. Ideas condemned as immoral or destabilizing may become foundations of social progress. Religious dissent, abolitionism, labor organizing, opposition to war, advocacy for racial equality, and demands for sexual freedom have all been treated in various societies as dangerous, indecent, or subversive. A censorship power created to suppress obvious falsehoods will eventually be used to suppress inconvenient facts.

The same problem applies to hate-speech laws. Hatred is contemptible, but its legal definition is inevitably political. Authorities must decide which groups are protected, what language counts as hateful, whether context matters, and when harsh criticism becomes unlawful hostility. Those decisions will reflect the values and interests of whoever holds power. A rule intended to protect vulnerable people may later be used against them: religious minorities may be prosecuted for criticizing dominant beliefs, activists may be accused of vilifying the police or the wealthy, and oppressed groups may be punished for expressing anger toward institutions that oppress them. Once censorship exists, there is no guarantee that benevolent officials will control it.

Absolute freedom of speech also recognizes the essential distinction between expression and conduct. The law may punish assault, vandalism, fraud, coercion, and other harmful acts without criminalizing the ideas associated with them. If someone commits violence, prosecute the violence. If someone cheats another person in a commercial transaction, prosecute the fraud. But the state should not punish a person simply for expressing hatred, repeating a false claim, endorsing a radical ideology, or insulting what others regard as sacred. Liberty requires judging people for what they do, not for what they think or say.

Critics argue that speech can itself inflict harm. This is true in an ordinary moral and psychological sense. Words can humiliate, intimidate, deceive, or inflame. Yet nearly every freedom permits conduct that can harm others in some way. Religious liberty permits doctrines that some consider oppressive. Freedom of association permits exclusion. Democratic participation permits citizens to support foolish or destructive policies. If the possibility of harm were sufficient to justify prohibition, no meaningful liberty could survive. A free society does not promise protection from every injury; it promises protection from coercive domination, especially domination by the state.

Misinformation presents a particularly tempting case for censorship because false claims can spread quickly and influence elections, public health, and social stability. But official suppression cannot solve the deeper problem of human fallibility. Governments themselves produce misinformation through propaganda, secrecy, error, and selective disclosure. Giving officials control over permissible truth would allow them to certify their own narratives and silence their critics. The proper response to falsehood is open investigation, independent journalism, education, public evidence, and vigorous counterargument—not legal prohibition.

Moreover, censorship often strengthens the ideas it seeks to destroy. Suppressed speakers can portray themselves as martyrs, while their claims migrate into secretive communities where they face less scrutiny. Open expression exposes bad ideas to criticism. It allows the public to identify extremists, examine their reasoning, challenge their evidence, and understand the grievances they exploit. Sunlight does not automatically defeat every lie, but darkness grants lies an aura of forbidden knowledge and protects them from examination.

An absolute approach also creates a clear and equal rule. Content-based exceptions invite selective enforcement because judgments about offensiveness, truth, and social danger are subjective. The powerful are better positioned than ordinary citizens to navigate vague laws, influence prosecutors, and define acceptable discourse. A simple prohibition against punishing expression denies officials that discretion. It protects everyone—not because every speaker deserves admiration, but because no authority deserves the power to license opinion.

This principle is especially important during emergencies. War, terrorism, epidemics, and civil unrest are precisely the moments when governments claim censorship is indispensable. They are also the moments when scrutiny is most necessary. Officials under pressure make grave errors and are most tempted to conceal them. A freedom that disappears whenever authorities declare a crisis is not a right but a temporary permission.

Defending absolute free speech does not require social indifference. Individuals, communities, publishers, and institutions may condemn hateful ideas, correct misinformation, refuse endorsement, organize protests, and support those targeted by abuse. It may answer speech, denounce it, ridicule it, and reject it—but it must not criminalize it. The cost of freedom is that people will say terrible things. The first cost is painful; the second is incompatible with a free society.

An absolutist interpretation of free speech rights—one that treats expression as presumptively protected in all circumstances and forbids carve-outs—offers the most coherent safeguard for liberty. 1) Freedom requires rules that do not depend on officials’ judgments

If free speech is protected only when government officials agree that a message is “acceptable,” then the right is not a right—it is a privilege granted at the pleasure of the powerful. The core value of constitutional liberty is not that speech survives the shifting preferences of officeholders; it is that speech survives disagreement with them.

Absolute free speech recognizes that officials are not neutral arbiters of truth or decency. They are fallible, biased, and incentivized to maintain authority. Once the state gains authority to suppress certain categories of expression—whether “hate speech,” “misinformation,” or “offensive content”—that authority inevitably expands. The threshold will always be elastic, because the justification (“harm,” “confusion,” “degradation,” “public disturbance”) can be applied to nearly anything that challenges dominant narratives or social hierarchies.

An absolutist rule refuses this entire game of discretionary judgment. It treats expressive freedom as a structural constraint on power, not a reward for speech that officials find congenial.

2) Exceptions create a mechanism for suppression that will be used broadly

The major objection to absolutism is typically that some expressions are too harmful to protect. But “harm” is precisely the category in which governments have historically been most eager to intervene. The reason is simple: harm is often difficult to measure in legal terms, yet easy to invoke politically. That makes harm an ideal tool for censorship.

If the law allows exceptions, then lawmakers will continually discover new reasons to classify speech into disfavored bins. Today the targets are “violent incitement” or “deceptive speech.” Tomorrow the targets become “disloyal speech,” “falsehoods that challenge national security,” or “extremist propaganda.” The history of censorship demonstrates that regimes do not merely misuse exceptions; they operationalize them. Once a state can punish expression because it deems it dangerous, the state no longer needs to wait for actual wrongdoing; it can act preemptively against ideas it dislikes.

An absolute approach blocks that trajectory. It denies government a foothold to regulate viewpoints through punitive legal categories.

3) Truth and falsity are not legally stable categories

Consider “misinformation.” The intuitive impulse is to punish speech that is factually wrong. But the very act of classifying misinformation presumes an institutional capacity for truth that governments rarely possess—and that courts often struggle to apply consistently.

First, knowledge evolves. Claims once dismissed as false may later be validated, while claims once treated as true can be overturned. Second, context matters: parody, satire, metaphor, and political rhetoric frequently rely on framing rather than strict factuality. Third, “misinformation” laws easily become “wrongthink” laws. When the state decides which statements count as misinformation, it inevitably privileges certain epistemic authorities and penalizes dissent from them.

An absolutist free speech standard avoids this problem by refusing to make legal doctrine a tribunal of contested facts. The remedy for error becomes persuasion and counter-speech—not legal coercion.

4) Offensive speech is part of the moral and political marketplace

Deeply offensive content challenges the comfort of the audience and can express contempt, cruelty, or humiliation. But offense alone is not a reliable moral basis for punishment. If the state is allowed to suppress speech because it is offensive, then the criteria for offensiveness will mirror prevailing social power: the tastes of majorities, the boundaries enforced by dominant norms, and the priorities of political coalitions.

Offense is also sometimes the signal of profound dissent. Many rights expansions in history—religious freedom, abolition, civil rights—were accompanied by speech that offended the status quo. If a society bans offensiveness as such, it bans exactly the rhetorical pressure that often precedes justice.

Absolutism therefore protects not merely pleasant expression but also the harshness of moral challenge. It recognizes that liberty is not measured by whether speech is agreeable; it is measured by whether the state can lawfully silence it.

5) “Hate speech” protections prevent government from enforcing social hierarchy

Arguments against protecting “hate speech” usually rely on the claim that certain expression degrades targeted groups and fosters harm. Yet a government empowered to outlaw hate speech must first define hate, then prove it, and then decide which expressions qualify. Those steps necessarily involve judgments about ideology, identity, and permissible social narratives.

The danger is that the state will become the enforcer of “acceptable” speech about social groups—using law to regulate whose dignity is protected, whose critique is tolerated, and whose viewpoints must be avoided. That is precisely the kind of state power that liberalism has historically tried to prevent.

Moreover, the censorship rationale assumes that punishing speech is an effective substitute for addressing real harm. But real harm is created through actions, not through ideas alone. The proper legal focus, in a rights-protective system, should be on conduct—threats, coercion, violence, harassment that crosses the legal line—rather than on suppressing viewpoints because they are morally repugnant. Absolutism goes further: it rejects the idea that the state should ever punish speech based on its content, no matter how hateful.

6) The remedy for dangerous ideas is not legal repression, but open contest

A durable theory of free speech rests on a political assumption: open expression enables society to correct errors, expose manipulation, and refine democratic self-government. This does not mean offensive or false speech is desirable; it means it must remain contestable in public rather than suppressible in courts.

Counter-speech, investigative journalism, educational institutions, and the free market of ideas are imperfect but less dangerous than censorship. Persuasion can be wrong, but it does not create an apparatus for coercion. Legal suppression, by contrast, turns disagreement into a criminal matter and gives the state a lasting role as ideological gatekeeper.

Absolutism thus offers a clean principle: when the government enters the marketplace of ideas as judge and punisher, it becomes easier to smuggle in power under the cover of protection.

7) Absolute protection better aligns with constitutional liberty than case-by-case balancing

“Balancing tests” and “intermediate scrutiny” approaches attempt to reconcile expression with competing interests. But balancing embeds uncertainty and discretion at the core of free speech doctrine. It invites judges and legislators to weigh the supposed value of speech against the supposed severity of harm, which will always depend on the political climate and the identities of speakers and audiences.

Absolutism replaces discretion with rule. A bright-line prohibition on suppressing expression based on content better protects against the selective enforcement that inevitably follows complex balancing standards. In practice, rights that depend on case-by-case evaluation tend to erode for unpopular groups, precisely because they are the easiest targets for officials.

If the Constitution is meant to secure liberty against governmental overreach, then the doctrine should not fluctuate according to cultural panic, election cycles, or prevailing moral fashions.

8) Preventing tyranny requires limiting the state’s most powerful tools

Tyranny is rarely announced as tyranny. It arrives through “reasonable” restrictions. Laws designed to “protect the public” and “maintain order” often become mechanisms for eliminating dissent. That is why an absolutist interpretation is not naïve: it is prophylactic. It understands that the most effective defense against authoritarian drift is to deny the state discretionary authority over viewpoint-based suppression.

Under an absolute approach, the state can still punish criminal conduct—threats, fraud in certain contexts, assault, coercion, and other behavior where the harm is direct and provable. But it cannot punish the existence of an idea simply because it is false, hateful, or offensive. The line preserves the crucial distinction between wrongdoing and expression, and it prevents government from using speech regulation as a proxy for punishing dissent.

Conclusion

Absolute free speech protection is not a defense of cruelty or error as values; it is a defense of liberty as a governing principle. When the state can create exceptions for hate speech, misinformation, or offensive content, it inevitably acquires the power to decide which viewpoints may live and which must die. That is the essence of tyranny: governance that rests on discretionary suppression rather than on equal rights.

An absolutist interpretation therefore safeguards freedom more effectively than any exception-based approach. It preserves the rule that citizens may speak—even when their speech is ugly, wrong, or socially disruptive—because the alternative grants government a gatekeeping role that will sooner or later be used against political opponents and unpopular communities. In a free society, the cure for offensive and false ideas is open contest, not legal annihilation. Absolute protection is the only doctrine robust enough to keep that contest genuinely free.
