The Case for Absolute Free Speech: A Bulwark Against Tyranny

Introduction

Free speech is the cornerstone of a free society. Without it, no other liberty can survive. Yet, in an era of growing censorship, moral panic, and governmental overreach, the principle of absolute free speech—where all expression, no matter how offensive, hateful, or false, is legally protected—has come under attack. Critics argue that hate speech, misinformation, and deeply offensive content should be regulated or banned to prevent harm. But such restrictions are not merely misguided; they are dangerous. They erode the foundations of liberty, empower the state to suppress dissent, and pave the way for tyranny. The only true safeguard against oppression is an absolute, unconditional right to free speech—one that permits all expression, no matter how repugnant, without exception.

The Moral and Philosophical Case for Absolute Free Speech

1. Speech is Intrinsically Valuable, Not Merely Instrumental

Many defenders of free speech argue that it should be protected because it leads to truth, democracy, and social progress. While these are valid points, they reduce speech to a mere means rather than recognizing it as an end in itself. The philosopher John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty, argued that even false or harmful speech must be permitted because: > "The peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation; those who dissent from the opinion, still more than those who hold it."

But this is not just about utility—it is about human dignity. Speech is how individuals express their thoughts, challenge authority, and define their identities. To deny someone the right to speak—even if their words are abhorrent—is to treat them as less than fully human, as a subject rather than a sovereign individual. No government has the right to dictate what thoughts are permissible.

2. The Slippery Slope of Censorship

History shows that once governments gain the power to suppress speech, they will abuse it. The moment we allow exceptions—"hate speech," "misinformation," "offensive content"—we create a precedent for further restrictions. What begins as banning "dangerous" speech quickly expands to silencing political opponents, religious minorities, and unpopular ideas.

  • Nazi Germany banned "degenerate" art and "subversive" books before moving on to Jewish, communist, and dissident voices.
  • The Soviet Union criminalized "anti-Soviet propaganda" before extending it to any criticism of the state.
  • Modern "hate speech" laws in Europe and Canada have been used to prosecute not just neo-Nazis, but also Christians, Muslims, and even satirists who offend dominant ideological groups.

If we permit the state to decide what is "acceptable" speech, we invite arbitrary power. The only way to prevent this is to ban all speech bans—to recognize that no idea, no matter how vile, should be subject to legal punishment.

3. The Marketplace of Ideas is Self-Correcting

Opponents of absolute free speech argue that harmful speech should be suppressed because it causes real-world damage—inciting violence, spreading lies, or fostering discrimination. But this ignores the self-regulating nature of free debate.

  • Bad ideas fail in the marketplace of ideas. If a speaker promotes hate, their audience will either reject them or, in a free society, counter them with better arguments. Censorship does not refute bad ideas—it hides them, allowing them to fester underground.
  • Audience accountability matters more than government censorship. If a speaker’s words lead to violence, the speaker (or their enablers) should face consequences—through social ostracization, economic boycotts, or criminal charges for actions, not words. But the state has no business acting as an arbiter of truth.
  • Suppressing speech does not eliminate it—it radicalizes it. When governments ban extremist groups, they drive them underground, where they become more violent and less accountable. Open debate, by contrast, allows moderates to engage with and dismantle radical ideas.

4. The Danger of Moral and Political Orthodoxy

One of the most insidious threats to free speech is the tyranny of the majority. When a dominant ideological or cultural group decides what is "acceptable" speech, dissenters—whether they be conservatives, libertarians, religious minorities, or unpopular thinkers—are silenced.

  • Campus speech codes often ban "microaggressions" or "triggering" speech, effectively muzzling political and religious minorities.
  • Social media censorship (e.g., Twitter/X, Facebook, YouTube) has led to the deplatforming of not just hate groups, but also journalists, scientists, and political figures who challenge dominant narratives.
  • Corporate and institutional boycotts (e.g., against "problematic" speakers) create a chilling effect, where people self-censor to avoid backlash.

If we allow the state—or private actors acting as de facto censors—to decide what is "harmful" speech, we risk creating a new orthodoxy, one where only approved ideas are permitted. The only way to prevent this is to reject all prior restraints on speech.

The Legal and Historical Precedent for Absolute Free Speech

1. The First Amendment’s Absolute Language

The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution states: > "Congress shall make no law… abridging the freedom of speech."

The wording is absolute. It does not say, "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech, except for hate speech, misinformation, and incitement." It is a blanket prohibition on government censorship.

Courts have occasionally carved out exceptions (e.g., "fighting words," "incitement to imminent lawless action"), but these exceptions are judicially created loopholes, not constitutional mandates. The original public meaning of the First Amendment was that no speech could be criminalized—only actions (e.g., violence, fraud, theft) could be punished.

2. The English Common Law Tradition

Before the First Amendment, English common law recognized that only actions, not words, could be punished. The 1644 Licensing Order (which imposed prior restraints on printing) was famously opposed by John Milton in Areopagitica, who argued: > "Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties."

This principle—that truth and falsehood should compete in the open market of ideas—was a cornerstone of Anglo-American legal thought. The 1791 Sedition Act (which criminalized "false, scandalous, and malicious" speech against the government) was widely condemned, and Thomas Jefferson (then in exile) argued that it was a violation of natural rights.

3. The European Counterexample: Why "Hate Speech" Laws Fail

Many European countries have hate speech laws, which criminalize speech that incites discrimination or violence based on race, religion, or sexual orientation. While well-intentioned, these laws have failed in practice:

  • They are selectively enforced. Far-right and Islamist extremists are prosecuted, but left-wing hate (e.g., anti-white racism, transphobic rhetoric from certain feminist groups) often goes unpunished.
  • They chill legitimate debate. Academics, journalists, and activists self-censor to avoid legal trouble, leading to a stifling of dissent.
  • They empower authoritarianism. In Hungary, Poland, and Turkey, hate speech laws have been used to silence political opponents rather than protect minorities.

The lesson is clear: No government can be trusted to define "hate" without abusing the power.

The Practical Consequences of Absolute Free Speech

1. It Protects the Weakest Voices

Absolute free speech is not just about protecting controversial speech—it protects dissident speech. History shows that minorities, heretics, and unpopular movements are the first to be silenced when speech restrictions are introduced.

  • Atheists, blasphemers, and religious dissenters (e.g., Salman Rushdie, the authors of The Satanic Verses) have faced death threats and bans under "blasphemy" laws.
  • LGBTQ+ activists in some countries are criminalized for "promoting homosexuality."
  • Journalists and whistleblowers (e.g., Julian Assange, Edward Snowden) are prosecuted under espionage laws for exposing government crimes.

If we allow any speech to be banned, we risk all speech being banned—especially that of those who challenge power.

2. It Forces Society to Confront Truth, Not Suppress It

Suppressing "misinformation" does not make falsehoods disappear—it drives them underground, where they spread unchecked. The only antidote to bad ideas is better ideas.

  • During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments and tech companies suppressed legitimate scientific debate (e.g., the lab-leak theory, early treatment options like Ivermectin). The result? Distrust in institutions, conspiracy theories, and polarization.
  • In the Soviet Union, dissent was crushed, but corruption and inefficiency festered because no one could speak truth to power.
  • In modern academia, cancel culture and deplatforming have led to intellectual conformity, where only approved narratives are permitted.

Absolute free speech forces society to engage with uncomfortable truths rather than bury them.

3. It Prevents Government Overreach

The greatest threat to liberty is not speech—it is the state. When governments gain the power to define and punish "harmful" speech, they inevitably abuse it.

  • China’s "social credit" system punishes "disruptive" speech with social and economic consequences.
  • Russia’s "foreign agent" laws criminalize independent journalism.
  • Canada’s "hate speech" prosecutions have targeted pastors, comedians, and even a 16-year-old girl for "transphobic" memes.

The only way to prevent this is to remove the power of censorship from the state entirely.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

1. "But Hate Speech Causes Real Harm!"

While it is true that hateful speech can lead to violence and discrimination, the solution is not censorship—it is consequences.

  • Incitement to violence should be punished as a crime, not as "speech."
  • Defamation and fraud should be litigated in civil courts, not criminalized.
  • Social ostracization and economic boycotts are far more effective than government bans.

Censorship does not stop harm—it hides it, making it harder to address.

2. "What About Misinformation During a Pandemic?"

The argument that false information about COVID-19 or vaccines should be suppressed is dangerous for two reasons:

  1. Who decides what is "misinformation"? Governments and tech companies have banned legitimate scientific debate while allowing state propaganda (e.g., Wuhan lab denials, vaccine mandates) to go unchallenged.
  2. Suppressing debate leads to worse outcomes. When Ivermectin and early treatment options were censored, millions died because alternative views were not permitted.

The only way to ensure truth prevails is to allow all ideas to compete.

3. "But Some Speech is So Offensive It Should Be Banned!"

Offensiveness is subjective. What one person finds deeply offensive, another may find inspiring or true.

  • Blasphemy laws have been used to silence atheists and religious critics.
  • "Hate speech" laws have been used to punish political opponents.
  • Morality police (e.g., in Iran, Saudi Arabia) jail people for "indecency."

If we allow the government to decide what is "offensive," we invite tyranny.

Conclusion: Absolute Free Speech as the Only True Liberty

The principle of absolute free speech—where no idea, no matter how vile, is legally punishable—is not just a legal doctrine. It is the foundation of human freedom.

  • It prevents government tyranny by removing the power of censorship.
  • It protects dissenters and minorities from being silenced by the majority.
  • It forces society to confront truth rather than suppress it.
  • It ensures that no idea is beyond challenge, which is the only way to prevent intellectual stagnation.

The alternative—gradual censorship, "hate speech" laws, and moral panic—leads to oppression, not progress. History has shown that once the state gains the power to suppress speech, it will use that power against everyone.

The only true safeguard against tyranny is absolute free speech—no exceptions, no carve-outs, no compromises. Anything less is a slippery slope to oppression.

As Voltaire (often misquoted) famously said: > "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it."

That is the essence of liberty. And liberty is worth defending—absolutely.

The Imperative of Absolute Free Speech: A Defense Without Exception

Introduction

Few principles in political philosophy have been more thoroughly tested, more consistently honored by free societies, and more frequently betrayed by governments in moments of moral panic than the principle of absolute free expression. Yet in an era of rising authoritarianism on both the political left and right, in which calls to censor "hate speech," "misinformation," and "harmful" content have become commonplace, the case for uncompromising speech protection deserves to be made with renewed vigor. The argument here is not that speech is always pleasant, never hurtful, or without social cost. It is, rather, that the alternative to absolute protection—the empowering of government to define the boundaries of acceptable expression—is far more dangerous to human liberty, human dignity, and human flourishing than any harm speech itself could ever inflict. The first principle of a free society is that government must never hold the power to decide what may be said.

I. The Historical Record: Censorship as a Tool of Tyranny

History offers no more consistent lesson than this: every system of state-controlled speech, without exception, has been turned against the vulnerable, the dissident, and the truth-seeker. The Roman Catholic Inquisition, the English licensing acts, the Soviet gulags, the Chinese Cultural Revolution, the Nazi book burnings, and the McCarthyite blacklist all share a common architecture—a government determining which ideas are permissible, and punishing those who deviate.

What is striking is not merely that these regimes targeted their obvious enemies, but that they consistently began by prohibiting speech that most citizens already found repugnant. Censorship rarely begins with the protection of a tyrant; it begins with the suppression of an extremist, a heretic, a "dangerous" thinker whose views the broad public already finds unacceptable. The comfort this provides is precisely what makes the precedent so dangerous. Once the state acquires the power to silence the fringe, the unpopular, the offensive, that power is inevitably extended to silence the merely inconvenient, then the dissenters, then the reformers.

Consider the Allied powers' internment of Japanese Americans, much of it justified by wartime speech restrictions. Consider the persecution of the Hollywood Ten, whose actual political beliefs often had little to do with their punishment—what mattered was that they refused to conform to state-mandated orthodoxy. Consider the more recent British treatment of Julian Assange, whose prosecution represents an extraordinary expansion of state power over journalism. The pattern is unwavering: when government may silence, government will silence, and those silenced will rarely be the powerful.

II. The Impossibility of Neutral Speech Regulation

Perhaps the most devastating argument against exceptions to free speech protection is the simple recognition that no human institution possesses the wisdom, the impartiality, or the foresight to distinguish "permissible" from "impermissible" expression reliably. Every attempt to define "hate speech" in law immediately confronts irresolvable questions: which groups are protected? Is criticism of Islam equivalent to criticism of Christianity? Is scientific inquiry into group differences permitted, however controversial? Is artistic expression that includes racial slurs acceptable in quotation but not in depiction? The answers to these questions are not technical legal matters; they are deeply contested political questions that vary by era, by culture, by the ideological composition of the courts and legislatures that must adjudicate them.

When the United Kingdom expanded its hate speech laws, the result was the prosecution of a man for a Facebook video criticizing immigration, a comedian investigated for a joke, and a teenager arrested for a rap lyric. The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal has compelled citizens to fund speech they find religiously offensive. Germany's enforcement of Holocaust-denial laws has been used to muzzle historical revisionism of all political stripes. The lesson is not that the people enforcing these laws are uniquely malicious—it is that the laws themselves, by their nature, capture vast domains of legitimate expression.

The categories themselves—"misinformation," "hate speech," "harmful content"—are not stable descriptors but contested political concepts. "Misinformation" in 1980 might include the proposition that AIDS was not caused by a virus. "Misinformation" in 2000 included the suggestion that mask mandates had costs as well as benefits. "Misinformation" in 2020 included concerns about vaccine safety that proved partially justified. The "experts" and "authorities" who define the boundaries of acceptable expression are themselves fallible, partisan, and embedded in the political conflicts of their time. To vest them with the power to silence dissent is to elevate their fallibility to a constitutional principle.

III. The Marketplace of Ideas and the Corruption of Truth by Authority

The classical liberal defense of free speech—the argument from the marketplace of ideas—is more compelling today than when John Stuart Mill first articulated it in On Liberty. Mill's insight was that human beings are incapable of knowing, in advance, which ideas are true and which are false. The only reliable mechanism for approaching truth is the adversarial testing of ideas in open competition, where the bad drives out the good only when the good has been fully and fairly articulated. To silence any view in advance is to assume that the silencing party already possesses complete knowledge—and history has taught us, repeatedly, that the opposite is the case.

But the marketplace of ideas argument goes further. Even when the "expert consensus" is genuinely correct on a particular question, the suppression of dissent corrupts the very institutions that produced the consensus. Science advances not by protecting orthodoxies but by subjecting them to continual challenge. The physicians who advocated hand-washing in the nineteenth century were ridiculed for decades. The meteorologists who proposed continental drift were dismissed as cranks. The epidemiologists who questioned specific pandemic measures operated within a long and noble tradition of scientific skepticism. When government enforces scientific consensus with the force of law, science itself becomes politicized, since the question is no longer "what is true" but "what has the state declared to be true." This is how the Lysenko affair destroyed Soviet biology for a generation. It is how the institutional credibility of public health has been eroded in our own time by the perception that dissenting views were not merely refuted but suppressed.

IV. The Coercion Inherent in State Speech Control

There is a deeper, more fundamental reason to reject all exceptions to free speech protection: state-imposed speech control is itself a form of violence. When the state prohibits a book, arrests a speaker, fines a publisher, or compels a citizen to speak against their conscience, it is employing the threat of force to control what human beings are permitted to think and articulate. This is true regardless of how enlightened, well-intentioned, or democratically mandated the prohibition may be.

Consider the implications of accepting even the most benign exceptions. If the state may prohibit speech that is "hateful" toward a racial group, it may prohibit the speech of Black nationalists as readily as white supremacists—and indeed, when the European Union and other bodies apply hate speech laws, this is precisely what happens. If the state may prohibit speech that "incites violence," it may prohibit the rhetoric of revolutionary movements that have historically been the only vehicle of liberation for oppressed peoples—including, notably, the American revolutionaries themselves, the abolitionists, the civil rights movement, and the anti-apartheid struggle. If the state may prohibit "misinformation," it may prohibit the revelations of whistleblowers whose information the state has classified as sensitive but which the public has a right to know.

Each exception, taken in isolation, may seem reasonable. The cumulative effect of all of them, however, is to construct a system in which the state holds a near-monopoly on legitimate public discourse, and the citizen is reduced to reciting whatever the authorities have determined to be acceptable. This is not a hypothetical danger; it is the lived reality of approximately four billion people on earth today.

V. The Counterargument Considered

It is worth confronting the strongest objection: surely, the critic asks, there must be limits? Surely, in a civilized society, we cannot permit the incitement to genocide, the targeted harassment of identifiable individuals, or the dissemination of dangerous falsehoods? Surely, the state has some legitimate role in protecting its citizens from communicative harm?

The response is not to deny the seriousness of these harms, but to insist that the cure is worse than the disease. Every censorship regime has been justified by reference to extraordinary harm—the incitement of hatred, the corruption of youth, the threat of revolution, the endangerment of public health. The harms are always real. The regimes are always disastrous. This is because the question is not whether the prohibited speech causes harm, but who shall be trusted with the power to define and prohibit it. The record is clear: that power will be abused, extended, and turned against the very people it was meant to protect.

Furthermore, the assumption that censorship actually works to reduce harm is empirically weak. Censorship rarely succeeds in suppressing ideas; it succeeds mainly in driving them underground, where they fester unchallenged, and in providing them with the seductive power of the forbidden. The actual historical record suggests that open, robust debate has been far more effective at discrediting hateful and false ideas than any prohibition. The American Ku Klux Klan reached its peak of influence not in an era of censorship but in an era of public confrontation with its ideas. The flat-earth movement thrives on YouTube not because it is censored but because it is permitted and refuted. The suppression of ideas rarely eliminates them; it merely immunizes them from the criticism that would expose their weaknesses.

VI. The Asymmetry of Risks

The fundamental case for absolute free speech protection is an argument from asymmetry. The risks of robust free speech are real but limited: some people will be offended, some will be misled, some will be radicalized. The risks of censorship are catastrophic and unbounded: a state with the power to define acceptable expression is a state that can silence every reform, every whistleblower, every minority, every dissenter, every truth that the powerful find inconvenient.

A free society that tolerates some bad speech is a society in which the truth may yet emerge, the powerless may yet organize, and the state may yet be held accountable. A censored society that prohibits some bad speech is a society in which the bad speech is replaced by whatever the state has determined to be true, and the citizen becomes merely a mouthpiece for the powerful. The choice is not between free speech and safety; it is between a world in which the truth may eventually be heard and a world in which the truth is whatever the authorities declare it to be.

VII. Toward a Culture of Free Expression

If the case for absolute free speech is compelling, the practical implications are profound. It means that platforms, institutions, and individuals must adopt a presumption in favor of expression, even when that expression is hateful, offensive, or false. It means that the response to bad speech must be more speech, better speech, more education, more criticism, and more courage—not state prohibition. It means accepting that the price of liberty is the constant exposure to ideas that one finds repugnant, and that this price, however high, is far lower than the price of the alternative.

The defense of free speech is not a defense of any particular idea, nor a defense of the right to be comfortable. It is a defense of the foundational condition under which human beings may think, speak, organize, and seek the truth. Once that condition is compromised—no matter how necessary, how urgent, how well-intentioned the compromise—the work of recovering it may take generations, and the harm done in the interim may be incalculable.

Conclusion

The absolute protection of free speech is not a position that emerges from indifference to the harms of hateful, false, or offensive expression. It emerges from a sober assessment of the historical record, a recognition of human fallibility, an understanding of the corrupting nature of state power, and a clear-eyed commitment to the principle that the freedom to speak is the freedom from which all other freedoms flow. A society that protects all speech, even the speech it despises, is a society that has preserved the capacity to recognize and confront its own errors. A society that prohibits some speech, even the speech that seems most dangerous, is a society that has begun the long and nearly irreversible descent into the darkness of state control over the human mind. The choice could not be clearer, and the responsibility to make it correctly could not be greater.

2. The "Who Decides" Problem If the state can silence speech deemed harmful, someone must determine what counts as harmful. Absolutists argue that this gatekeeping power, no matter how benevolently intended, becomes a tool that the powerful use to entrench themselves. As the saying goes, "free speech for me but not for thee" is the natural tendency of any speech-restriction regime.

Core Arguments

The Slippery Slope / Entrenchment of Power

The most-cited argument is historical: every modern speech restriction, absolutists claim, was originally defended with the "right" exceptions in mind, then expanded.

  • War powers exceptions in WWI produced the Espionage Act prosecutions of Eugene Debs and the Schenck "clear and present danger" test.
  • "Fighting words" doctrine, narrowed in Chaplinsky, has been stretched to cover broader categories.
  • Incitement laws, designed for imminent lawless action, have been applied to protest, dissent, and even journalism.

The argument is not that any individual restriction is obviously tyrannical, but that the cumulative trajectory of speech regulation gives the state a powerful lever against its critics. Once the tool exists, it gets used.

The Marketplace of Ideas / Mill's Argument

John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859) is the philosophical cornerstone. Mill argued that:

  • Even if a silenced view is true, suppressing it prevents society from understanding why it is true, leaving people with dogmatic belief rather than reasoned conviction.
  • If the suppressed view contains any partial truth, silencing it forfeits that contribution.
  • Even if the view is entirely false, the collision with error helps clarify and strengthen the true view.

The supposed benefit: truth that has been "stress-tested" against opposition is more robust than truth protected from challenge. Misinformation, in this view, is best defeated by better information in open debate—not by removing it from the field.

The Chilling Effect

Absolutists argue that any speech restriction, even a narrow one, creates legal uncertainty. People self-censor not just what is clearly forbidden but anything adjacent to it. The result is that controversial but legitimate speech—political dissent, whistleblowing, unpopular scientific findings, minority viewpoints—disappears first, because those expressing it are least able to afford legal defense.

The ACLU, in its famous 1978 defense of neo-Nazis' right to march in Skokie, Illinois, articulated this clearly: once you create a class of speech the government can prohibit because it is "too hurtful," you have created a weapon that will eventually be turned against the groups you most want to protect.

The Protection of Minorities

Absolutists reverse the usual framing of "hate speech laws protect minorities" and argue the opposite: speech restrictions historically and structurally target minorities and dissidents.

  • Authoritarian regimes justify censorship by claiming to protect the public from "harmful" ideas.
  • In democratic societies, majority opinion often defines what counts as offensive, and minorities—by definition—hold views the majority dislikes.
  • The communities most burdened by vague hate speech or "misinformation" standards have often been religious minorities (e.g., Catholic politicians on abortion), anti-war activists, civil rights protesters, labor organizers, and sexual minorities defending themselves against prevailing social norms.

The supposed benefit: a regime of absolute protection prevents the state from picking which voices count as "acceptable."

The Distinction Between Speech and Action

A central claim is that words are not violence and do not equal incitement to imminent lawless action. Hate speech, no matter how repugnant, causes its harm only through interpretation and response. Treating it as a direct harm:

  • Collapses the distinction that makes liberal democratic order possible.
  • Empowers the state to define "harm" ever more expansively.
  • Removes the moral responsibility of listeners to evaluate claims critically.

From this view, the harms of hate speech are real but are addressed by counter-speech, social sanction, education, private action, and—when the line to action is crossed—existing incitement, harassment, and public accommodation laws.

Self-Correction Requires Open Channels

Closed information systems cannot self-correct. The Soviet Union, Maoist China, and other closed regimes held doctrinally "settled" views for decades while reality diverged catastrophically. Open systems, despite their noise and ugliness, generate error-correction: bad claims get challenged, refuted, exposed.

Misinformation, in this view, is a problem of information quality—addressed by better journalism, education, platform design, and institutions—not by removing the underlying speech, which simply pushes misinformation underground while degrading the open system that would have exposed it.

Dignity and Autonomy

Adults are moral agents capable of evaluating claims and choosing what to believe. Restricting speech treats citizens as children who must be shielded from certain ideas. The supposed benefit of absolutism is that it respects the autonomy and intellectual capacity of the citizenry—a respect that, paradoxically, may produce more thoughtful publics than paternalistic protection.

The Supposed Benefits Summarized

  1. Resistance to tyranny — keeps the state's silencing power minimal.
  2. Discovery of truth — robust, contested knowledge rather than protected orthodoxy.
  3. Protection of dissent — minorities, whistleblowers, and unpopular views can speak.
  4. Vibrant public discourse — more speech, not less, produces better outcomes.
  5. Epistemic humility — guards against the mistake of treating current consensus as final truth.
  6. Civic maturation — citizens practice critical thinking rather than relying on state gatekeeping.

Important Caveats

Most absolutists distinguish between:

  • Government action (which they oppose) and private action (which they generally defend, including social boycotts, employer discipline, and platform moderation).
  • Speech and true threats, fraud, or direct incitement (which they accept as legitimately regulable).
  • Protection of the right to speak and endorsement of the content—they will defend a speaker's right while despising the views.

This position is, of course, contested. Those who favor restrictions on hate speech and misinformation argue that the absolutist frame understates real harms, ignores power asymmetries, and mistakes a particular historical moment's political equilibrium for a permanent feature of human societies. But the absolutist position remains one of the major intellectual traditions in modern liberalism for the reasons outlined above.

Title: The Imperative of Absolute Free Speech: A Shield Against Tyranny and Guardian of Liberty

Introduction
Free speech is the cornerstone of a free society, acting as both a mirror reflecting human diversity and a weapon against oppression. To argue for absolute free speech—unfettered legal protection for all forms of expression, including hate speech, misinformation, and offensive content—is to champion the fundamental belief that liberty is best preserved when the state is stripped of the authority to dictate acceptable ideas. While critics may label this stance as perilous, history and philosophy demonstrate that restricting speech emboldens tyranny, stifles progress, and creates a society vulnerable to authoritarianism. By defending even the most contemptible expressions, we safeguard the very essence of democratic discourse and individual autonomy.

The Philosophical Foundation: Protecting Individual Autonomy
At its core, free speech is integral to human dignity. As John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty, even false or offensive ideas must be permitted, for the “conviction that truth is great and strong enough to bear unanimity” depends on its ability to confront opposing views. This exchange—chaotic and uncomfortable though it may be—is essential to discovering truth and fostering intellectual growth. To suppress thought, even abhorrent thought, is to delegitimize the individual’s capacity to discern and to choose. For true liberty, citizens must be free to offend, mislead, or enrage—because in doing so, they retain agency over their minds, unshackled by state mandates on what to believe or say.

Historical Precedent: The Perils of Government Control Over Speech
When governments claim the right to censor, tyranny follows. Nazi Germany’s book burnings, the Soviet Union’s purges of dissent, and authoritarian regimes’ suppression of minority voices all illustrate the dangers of state-mediated speech. In these contexts, censorship began with marginalized voices and escalated into broader oppression. Even in democracies, overreach lurks: the U.S. Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, which criminalized criticism of the government, demonstrate how elites exploit “harmful” rhetoric to silence opposition. These lessons underscore that any government authority to restrict speech is a step toward authoritarian control.

The Slippery Slope: Where Restrictions Lead
Today’s “common-sense” restrictions on hate speech or misinformation become tomorrow’s tools for political suppression. Who decides what constitutes “hate”? In 2022, European Union hate speech laws were weaponized by authoritarian-leaning leaders to silence critics; similar risks emerge when subjective offensiveness controls content. Moreover, the “harm” of offensive ideas is speculative: social harms can be addressed through education, counter-speech, and civil discourse, not legal punishment. Government intervention risks replacing nuanced dialogue with blunt censorship, eroding empathy and rational debate.

The Marketplace of Ideas: Trust in Humanity’s Judgment
The “marketplace of ideas” theory holds that truth emerges when all viewpoints, however odious, are permitted to compete. While hateful or false ideas may exist, their exposure under open scrutiny often reveals their weakness. For instance, the Ku Klux Klan’s public rallies in the U.S. have dwindled due to public censure, not legal prohibition. Similarly, misinformation on climate or medicine, though dangerous, thrives when suppressed (e.g., conspiracy theories about vaccines hidden in authoritarian contexts often gain more traction). Trusting citizens to evaluate ideas fosters resilience and innovation more than state-controlled narratives.

Misinformation and Democratic Discourse
Critics arguing that false speech undermines democratic discourse fail to recognize that transparency—including exposing error—is critical to accountability. Democratic societies must allow leaders and citizens to err; prohibition creates a false sense of security. Social media fact-checking and public scrutiny better address misinformation without empowering the state to become an arbiter of truth. History shows that “official” truths can be just as fallacious as unfettered speech (e.g., pseudoscientific claims once deemed credible).

Conclusion: A Call for Unflinching Freedom
In absolute free speech, we reject the seductive but perilous role of empowering governments to police ideas. The path of restrictions breeds authoritarianism, stifles growth, and demeans human judgment. Even offensive and harmful expressions must be legally shielded, for they are the price of preserving individual liberty and democratic integrity. The strength of free speech lies not in its comfort but in its capacity to protect us from the far-greater danger of tyranny. Let our laws reflect this wisdom, ensuring that no authority can silence the pen, the keyboard, or the voice—and thus, ensuring our perpetually free future.

    • Benefit: Preserves current freedoms indefinitely by preventing incremental erosion of speech protections.

    • Benefit: Promotes long-term societal resilience by letting people learn to engage with diverse, even repulsive, viewpoints.

Proponents respond to critiques by emphasizing that actions, not ideas, should be criminalized (e.g., incitement to violence). They argue that overregulation often backfires, and that historical progress on civil rights, for instance, required challenging restrictive norms through robust speech. Furthermore, restricting speech in one context can normalize authoritarian approaches, while open discourse builds stronger, more adaptable societies capable of rejecting harmful ideas through dialogue and consensus.

In summary, an absolutist free speech policy is seen as a bulwark against authoritarianism and government overreach, ensuring that even uncomfortable or offensive expressions remain protected to safeguard long-term democratic values and individual liberty.

The Absolutist Free Speech Perspective: Why All Speech Must Be Protected

The absolutist free speech position argues that any government restriction on expression, no matter how offensive, false, or harmful it seems, fundamentally undermines liberty and creates greater dangers than the speech itself. This view, most famously embodied in the strong interpretation of the US First Amendment (though not universally applied even there), rests on several core philosophical and practical pillars. Here's an explanation of its reasoning and supposed benefits from within that viewpoint:

Core Philosophical Foundations

  1. Speech as the Bedrock of Liberty & Human Dignity: Absolutists view the freedom to express thoughts, however unpopular or wrong, as inseparable from human autonomy and personhood. Restricting speech, even "bad" speech, is seen as treating individuals as children incapable of reasoning, denying their fundamental dignity as rational agents. Liberty isn't just about comfortable speech; it's defined by the protection of all speech.
  2. The Government as Inherently Untrustworthy Censor: The core belief is that governments (and powerful private entities acting with state sanction) are structurally prone to censorship for self-serving, political, or majoritarian reasons. Granting them the power to decide which speech is "too hateful" or "too false" is seen as inevitably leading to the suppression of dissent, minority viewpoints, and challenges to the status quo. History is replete with examples of "hate speech" or "misinformation" laws being used against civil rights activists, feminists, religious minorities, or political opponents.
  3. The Slippery Slope is Inevitable & Real: Absolutists argue there is no stable, neutral, or objective line between "protected" and "unprotected" speech once you start drawing exceptions. Classifying speech requires subjective judgments about:
    • What constitutes "hate"? (Offends whom? Based on whose sensibilities? How severe must the harm be?)
    • What is "misinformation"? (Who is the arbiter of "truth"? How complex must the issue be? Does it require deliberate malice?)
    • Where is the "imminent" harm threshold? (This is the only widely accepted exception in strong absolutist views - true threats or incitement to imminent lawless action). Once the principle that "some speech can be banned" is accepted, the categories inevitably expand. Today's "hate speech" could be tomorrow's "harmful misinformation," then "disrespectful speech," then "politically incorrect speech." The slope isn't theoretical; it's a documented historical pattern.

Supposed Benefits & Practical Reasoning (from the Absolutist View)

  1. Preventing Censorship Creep & Protecting Dissent: The primary supposed benefit is safeguarding the most important speech – criticism of the powerful, radical challenges to orthodoxy, and the speech of marginalized groups. Absolutists argue:
    • Today's "hate speech" against a minority might be tomorrow's civil rights movement slogan.
    • "Misinformation" labeled by the government today might be scientific truth uncovered tomorrow (e.g., germ theory, heliocentrism).
    • Laws banning "hate speech" are almost always weaponized first against political dissenters or unpopular minorities, not just generic bigots. Protecting all speech, including vile speech, creates a firewall that protects the speech society needs most.
  2. The "Marketplace of Ideas" Requires Unfettered Competition: Drawing from John Stuart Mill and Justice Holmes, absolutists believe truth is best discovered and society best served when all ideas compete freely. Suppressing even false or hateful ideas:
    • Prevents them from being openly refuted, allowing them to fester in secret and gain unchallenged power.
    • Robs society of the chance to strengthen true beliefs by confronting and defeating false ones ("He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that" - Mill).
    • Assumes the current "truth" is infallible, which history shows it is not. Protecting all speech ensures society constantly tests and refines its understanding.
  3. Empowering Citizens, Not Government: Absolutists trust individuals and civil society (counter-speech, boycotts, social pressure, education) to combat bad speech far more than they trust government bureaucracies or courts. The supposed benefit is:
    • Resilience: Citizens develop critical thinking and the ability to discern truth from falsehood through exposure and debate, not state protection.
    • Accountability: Groups promoting hate or lies face social and economic consequences without state intervention, which is seen as more legitimate and less prone to abuse.
    • Preventing Infantilization: Society doesn't become stronger by shielding people from ideas; it becomes stronger by equipping people to engage with and rebut them.
  4. Clarity, Predictability, and Judicial Restraint: A bright-line rule ("no restrictions except true threats/imminent incitement") is seen as:
    • Easier to Apply Consistently: Reduces arbitrary enforcement and costly litigation over fuzzy standards like "hate" or "misinformation."
    • Limiting Judicial Power: Prevents judges from becoming "Ministers of Thought," making subjective moral judgments about speech content. The law stays focused on conduct (inciting violence) not ideas.
  5. Epistemic Humility: A profound benefit is fostering societal humility about the certainty of current beliefs. Recognizing that even our most cherished "truths" could be wrong (or incomplete) and that today's fringe view could be tomorrow's consensus requires tolerating offensive or false speech. Silencing ideas based on current consensus stifles intellectual and social progress.

Addressing the Specific Concerns (Hate Speech & Misinformation)

  • Hate Speech: Absolutists argue:
    • The best remedy for hateful ideas is more speech – counter-speech, education, community building. Government bans often amplify the speaker ("martyr effect") and drive hatred underground.
    • Defining "hate" is inherently subjective and culturally/politically charged. Who decides what offends? Laws often target speech against dominant groups less effectively than speech against marginalized groups.
    • Physical violence or discrimination should be banned as conduct, but the ideas preceding them, however vile, must remain protected to avoid criminalizing thought and preventing the identification of genuine threats through open discourse.
  • Misinformation: Absolutists argue:
    • Distinguishing "misinformation" (unintentional error) from "disinformation" (deliberate falsehood) and from legitimate debate on complex issues is often impossible for the state.
    • Government labeling speech as "misinformation" is a massive expansion of state power with immense potential for abuse (e.g., labeling inconvenient science or political criticism as "false").
    • The solution is better information and critical thinking skills fostered by robust debate, not censorship. Suppressing "false" ideas doesn't make truth prevail; it just removes the opportunity to demonstrate why it's false.

The Core Mantra from This Viewpoint

"The remedy for bad speech is more speech, not enforced silence." Any restriction, however well-intentioned, grants the state dangerous power to suppress the very speech that is most vital for liberty, progress, and holding power accountable. The peril of a government empowered to ban "bad" ideas always outweighs the harm caused by the ideas themselves, which a free society is capable of confronting through debate, persuasion, and social action. True freedom requires tolerating the speech we despise the most, because the alternative is trusting fallible humans in power to decide what we are allowed to hear and say. The supposed benefit is not a comfortable society, but the strongest possible bulwark against tyranny and intellectual stagnation.

Core Reasons for Absolutist Free Speech

  1. The Slippery Slope Argument

    • Once exceptions to free speech are made (e.g., banning hate speech or "misinformation"), the justification for further restrictions expands.
    • History shows that what begins as a targeted ban on "extreme" speech often broadens to suppress dissent, political opposition, or unpopular but legitimate views.

  2. The Marketplace of Ideas

    • Originating from John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty, this theory argues that truth emerges from open debate. Bad ideas are best defeated by better ideas, not censorship.
    • If speech is restricted, society loses the opportunity to refute, expose, or learn from even the most objectionable ideas.
    • Censorship assumes that authorities (governments, platforms, or institutions) can reliably distinguish truth from falsehood—a premise absolutists reject as arrogant and fallible.

  3. Protection of Minority and Unpopular Views

    • Many now-accepted ideas (abolitionism, civil rights, LGBTQ+ rights) were once considered dangerous or immoral.
    • Restrictions on speech disproportionately harm marginalized groups, whose views are often suppressed by those in power.
    • Example: In the U.S., early labor organizers and civil rights activists were frequently arrested under "public order" laws for their speech.

  4. Distrust of Government and Institutional Power

    • Absolutists argue that no entity should have the authority to decide what speech is permissible.
    • Governments and powerful institutions are prone to abuse such power to silence criticism (e.g., authoritarian regimes using "hate speech" or "fake news" laws to jail opponents).
    • Even well-intentioned restrictions can be weaponized by future regimes with different values.

  5. The Chilling Effect

    • When speech is restricted, people self-censor out of fear of legal or social punishment, even if their speech is legally protected.
    • This stifles creativity, debate, and progress, as individuals avoid controversial but important discussions.
    • Example: Academics or journalists may avoid researching or reporting on sensitive topics if they fear repression.

  6. The Impracticality of Defining Harmful Speech

    • Hate speech: What counts as "hateful"? Is criticism of a religion or ideology different from an attack on a person? Definitions vary widely by culture and era.
    • Misinformation: Who decides what is "true"? Governments and tech platforms have bias and errors (e.g., suppression of early COVID-19 theories that later proved plausible).
    • Attempts to regulate speech often lead to arbitrary or politicized enforcement (e.g., social media bans targeting one political side over another).

  7. Moral Principle: Autonomous Individuals

    • Absolutists often hold that freedom of thought and expression is a fundamental human right, not subject to negotiation based on content.
    • The alternative—allowing restrictions—implies that some ideas are too dangerous for people to hear, which infantilizes citizens and assumes they cannot think critically.
    • As Evelyn Beatrice Hall (often misattributed to Voltaire) wrote: "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it."

  8. Historical Lessons

    • Authoritarian regimes (Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union, modern-day China) have consistently used speech restrictions to control populations.
    • Even in democracies, overbreadth in speech laws has led to abuses (e.g., the U.S. Sedition Act of 1918, used to jail anti-war activists).
    • Absolutists argue that free speech is the first line of defense against tyranny.

Supposed Benefits of Absolutist Free Speech

  1. Preservation of Fundamental Freedoms

    • If speech can be restricted for being "harmful" or "offensive," all other rights (assembly, press, religion) become vulnerable to similar justifications.
    • Free speech is often called the "first freedom" because it enables the protection of all other liberties.

  2. A Stronger, More Resilient Society

    • Exposure to a wide range of ideas—even bad ones—forces individuals to develop critical thinking and robust arguments.
    • Prohibiting speech does not eliminate the underlying beliefs; it only drives them underground, where they fester without scrutiny.

  3. Encouraging Accountability and Transparency

    • In an open society, bad actors are exposed to public scrutiny. Censorship can make it harder to identify and counter harmful movements.
    • Example: Allowing white supremacists to speak publicly enables journalistic investigation and public rebuttal, whereas driving them underground can make them harder to monitor.

  4. Fostering Innovation and Progress

    • Many scientific, political, and social breakthroughs initially challenged orthodoxy (e.g., heliocentrism, civil rights, gender equality).
    • Restrictions on speech can stifle unconventional but valid ideas before they gain traction.

From this perspective, the dangers of restricting speech outweigh the harm of allowing it. Even speech that is false, offensive, or hateful must be protected because:

The Absolute Necessity of Unrestricted Free Speech: Safeguarding Liberty Against Tyranny

Introduction

Free speech is the cornerstone of a free society. Without it, governments become tyrants, truth is suppressed, and individuals are reduced to subjects rather than citizens. Any exception to free speech—whether for "hate," "misinformation," or "offensiveness"—grants the state the power to decide what ideas are permissible, a power that has historically been used to crush dissent and enforce conformity.

I. Absolute Free Speech Prevents Governmental Tyranny

History demonstrates that the greatest threats to liberty come not from unchecked speech, but from governments that seek to control it. The 20th century alone saw regimes from Nazi Germany to Stalinist Russia to Maoist China use speech restrictions to justify mass repression. In each case, the state first targeted "dangerous" ideas—communism, fascism, religious dissent—and then expanded its censorship until no dissent remained.

The United States, in its founding documents, recognized this danger. As Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. famously wrote in Abrams v. If we allow exceptions for "hate speech," we create a slippery slope where the government—or activist courts—decide what constitutes "hate." Who defines it? The majority? A self-appointed moral elite? In Canada, "hate speech" laws have been used to prosecute individuals for expressing controversial religious or political views. In Europe, "denial of the Holocaust" is criminalized, yet historical revisionism is a legitimate (if controversial) academic pursuit. If the state can punish speech for being "offensive," then no idea is truly safe—only those approved by the ruling class.

The alternative—a world where the government decides which ideas are permissible—is one where dissent is criminalized, and tyranny thrives. Absolute free speech is the only safeguard against this.

II. Society Corrects Itself Through Open Debate, Not Censorship

A common argument against absolute free speech is that certain expressions—such as hate speech or misinformation—cause harm. But harm is not a valid justification for censorship in a free society. Instead, the best response to bad speech is more speech—better arguments, counter-narratives, and public shaming (when socially appropriate).

Consider the case of misinformation. Rather than banning false claims, society should encourage robust fact-checking, education, and debate. When the government suppresses dissenting views—such as scientific skepticism or alternative political theories—it does not eliminate the problem; it ensures that only one side of the argument is heard. This is how propaganda regimes function. The Soviet Union banned "anti-Soviet" speech, yet dissent persisted in underground samizdat publications. The more the state suppresses, the more it fuels underground resistance.

Similarly, "hate speech" laws do not eliminate hatred—they drive it underground. When white supremacists are prosecuted for their views, they retreat into encrypted forums where their ideas fester unchallenged. If instead, their arguments were openly debated and refuted in public discourse, their influence would weaken over time. The same is true for conspiracy theories: banning them only makes them more appealing to those who feel persecuted.

The market of ideas, as John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty, is self-correcting. Bad ideas fail when exposed to scrutiny; good ideas prevail when given the chance. Censorship, by contrast, ensures that only the state’s preferred narratives survive.

III. Absolute Free Speech Protects Unpopular Minorities from Mob Rule

One of the most dangerous consequences of speech restrictions is that they empower majorities to silence minorities. History shows that when governments grant themselves the power to censor, they often use it against the most vulnerable.

Consider the case of blasphemy laws, which criminalize insults to religion. In many Muslim-majority countries, apostasy is punishable by death. In India, cow slaughter laws have been used to persecute religious minorities. These laws are not enforced against the powerful but against those who lack political protection. The same is true of "hate speech" laws in Western democracies: they are disproportionately applied against marginalized groups whose speech is deemed "too offensive" by the dominant culture.

Absolute free speech ensures that even the most despised ideas can be expressed, no matter how offensive. This is not to say that such speech should be encouraged or amplified, but that it should not be criminalized. The alternative—a world where the state or mob decides what is permissible—is one where dissent is impossible, and tyranny waits just around the corner.

IV. The Slippery Slope of Speech Restrictions

Opponents of absolute free speech often argue that exceptions are necessary to prevent immediate harm. But history shows that every exception leads to further restrictions. The path from "hate speech" laws to thought crime is short.

  • Germany’s "Volksverhetzung" (incitement to hatred) laws were initially used to prosecute neo-Nazis but have since been applied to critics of immigration and even to satirists.
  • France’s "denial of crimes against humanity" laws have been used to prosecute historians who question official narratives.
  • Canada’s "hate speech" provisions have led to prosecutions of individuals for expressing controversial religious or political views.

Once the government gains the power to suppress speech it deems harmful, it will inevitably expand that power. The only way to prevent this is to draw a bright-line rule: No speech shall be restricted by the state.

V. The Moral Case for Absolute Free Speech

Beyond the practical arguments, there is a moral case for absolute free speech: the right to express oneself is an inalienable human liberty.

Every person has the right to speak their mind, no matter how foolish, offensive, or dangerous their words may seem. To deny this right is to treat individuals as less than free agents—capable only of thinking what the state approves.

Even if we accept that some speech causes harm, the harm of censorship is far greater. When the government suppresses speech, it sends a message: Your ideas are not welcome here. This creates a chilling effect, where people fear speaking their minds, even on benign topics. Over time, this erodes trust in institutions and fosters a culture of conformity.

Moreover, absolute free speech is the only framework that respects the dignity of every individual. It does not require that we like what others say, only that we allow them to say it. This is the essence of a free society—one where no one is forced to listen, but no one is forced to remain silent.

Conclusion: Free Speech Must Be Absolute

The case for absolute free speech is not about defending hate, misinformation, or offensive content for its own sake. It is about defending the principle that no idea should be beyond the reach of debate—because when the government decides which ideas are permissible, it is no longer a government of laws but a government of men.

History has shown that speech restrictions lead to tyranny, that censorship does not eliminate bad ideas but drives them underground, and that the only way to protect unpopular minorities is to ensure that no one—no matter how despised—can be permanently silenced. The First Amendment was not written to protect popular opinions but to protect all opinions, even the most unpopular ones, because in a free society, the right to speak is not a privilege to be granted but a liberty to be defended.

If we surrender even an inch of free speech, we risk losing it all. The only safe path is absolute protection—no exceptions, no qualifications, no carve-outs. Anything less is a step toward the very tyranny we claim to oppose.
